analysis.one_liner: Taxes excess oil and gas profits and uses the money to cut transit fares and reward fuel-efficient cars.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 66 cosponsors in the House, but committees never acted on it and it expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have taxed profits on oil and natural gas sales that exceed what a new Reasonable Profits Board judged reasonable — at rates from 50% up to 100% of the excess. The money would fund two things for consumers: income tax credits up to $6,000 for buying very fuel-efficient cars assembled in the U.S. by union workers, and federal grants to bus and commuter rail systems to reduce passenger fares. It was introduced during the 2008 gas price spike.
analysis.who_benefits: Commuters and drivers facing high gas prices: mass transit riders would get lower fares, buyers of fuel-efficient American-made cars would get credits up to $6,000, and if the windfall tax restrained oil price spikes, everyone who buys fuel would benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, transit riders, and fuel-efficient car buyers

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax on oil and gas profits above a board-determined reasonable profit, at 50% of the excess between 100–102% of reasonable profit, 75% between 102–105%, and 100% above 105% [S3].
Creates a tax credit of up to $3,000, $4,500, or $6,000 for buying passenger vehicles in the top tiers of fuel economy, if assembled in the U.S. under a collective bargaining agreement [S3].
Authorizes grants to bus and commuter rail operators to reduce fares equally for all passengers, funded by the windfall tax revenue left over after paying for the vehicle credit [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers and refiners would pay the windfall tax on profits above the board's benchmark; to the extent sellers pass the tax through, drivers would pay somewhat more at the pump.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers, possibly drivers via pass-through

drawbacks.text: An excise tax on oil and gas sales is typically paid by the seller, so producers could pass some or all of it to consumers in higher fuel prices, partially offsetting the relief the bill aims to provide [S3].

Letting a three-member presidentially appointed board define 'reasonable profit' case by case gives an unelected body wide discretion over a major tax, and the bill takes effect on enactment with no transition time for companies to adjust [S3].

The vehicle credit is limited to cars assembled in the U.S. under a collective bargaining agreement, which excludes imported fuel-efficient vehicles and non-union U.S. plants and would raise the cost of the credit relative to a fuel-economy-only design [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the upside was direct: cheaper transit fares and credits worth up to $6,000 toward a fuel-efficient car during a period when gas prices were a top household concern. The main cost risk is pass-through of the windfall tax to pump prices, which could erode or outweigh the benefits for drivers, and the board's broad discretion makes the tax's reach uncertain. The union-assembly restriction makes the credit both costlier and narrower than a simple efficiency incentive.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2008 and sent to two House committees, but neither committee ever took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 8, 2008 by Rep. Kucinich with 65 original cosponsors [S1,S3].
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day of introduction [S1,S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit, and no further action — no markup, no floor vote — was ever recorded [S5].
The bill accumulated 66 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill expired without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies avoided the windfall tax entirely, and no one else gained from the bill's death; commuters and car buyers never saw the fares or credits it promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers who avoided the tax

sides.party_line_note: All 67 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill and no vote ever occurred.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would tax up to 100% of profits exceeding a board-set reasonable benchmark, directly cutting into the industry's record 2008-era earnings. Its interest in the bill's failure ran directly against consumers who were paying the resulting pump prices.

The vehicle credit is restricted to cars assembled in the U.S. under a collective bargaining agreement, channeling up to $6,000 per sale toward unionized domestic plants. Buyers also benefit, so the industry's interest here runs alongside consumers'.

industries.industry: Imported-car makers and non-union U.S. plants
industries.note: The credit excludes their vehicles regardless of fuel economy, putting them at a price disadvantage against unionized domestic competitors even when selling more efficient cars.
Federal grants would fund fare reductions for all riders, easing the cost pressure transit systems face when fuel prices spike and ridership rises.
